title: Krka National Park: Is It Worth Visiting in 2027?
metaDescription: A complete, fact-based guide to visiting Krka National Park in 2027. Covers the €40 entrance fee, crowds, swimming ban, and if it is worth the trip.
content:
## Understanding the 2027 Entrance Fees

Krka National Park operates on a tiered pricing system that fluctuates dramatically based on the month. During the peak summer season from June through September, adult admission costs €40. Children between the ages of seven and eighteen enter for €15, while children under seven enter free of charge year-round.

During the shoulder season months of April, May, and October, the adult ticket price drops by half to €20, and children's tickets cost €10. In the winter months from November through March, access is heavily discounted to €7 for adults and €4 for children.

These base tickets grant access to all land sites within the 109-square-kilometer park. This includes the main Skradinski Buk boardwalks, the Roški Slap area, the Krka Eco Campus in Puljane, and the Burnum Roman ruins. The ticket also covers mandatory internal transport connecting the entry gates to the main trails. From April to October, this includes the ferry from the town of Skradin to Skradinski Buk and the shuttle buses operating from the Lozovac parking lot down to the trailhead.

It is important to note that the base ticket does not cover the longer, optional boat excursions within the park. Traveling by boat from Skradinski Buk to Visovac Island or Roški Slap requires an additional fee. A standard two-hour round trip to Visovac Island costs an extra €15 for adults.

## The Swimming Ban and Its Impact

For decades, Krka National Park was heavily marketed as the only major waterfall park in Croatia where visitors could swim. This changed on January 1, 2021, when park authorities enacted a permanent ban on swimming at Skradinski Buk.

The ban was implemented to protect the delicate travertine barriers, which are created by calcium carbonate depositing onto moss and algae. The sheer volume of swimmers, combined with the chemical residue from sunscreen, had degraded the water quality and disrupted the ecosystem.

Paying €40 during the peak of July and August is difficult to justify when the boardwalks are completely logjammed and swimming in the main falls is permanently prohibited. Visitors expecting to wade into the turquoise pools directly beneath the main cascade often arrive unaware of the current regulations.

Swimming is now restricted to three specific areas further upstream: Roški Slap, Stinice, and Pisak. These designated zones are open for swimming from June 1 to September 30, dependent on water levels. Alternatively, many visitors choose to swim at the public beach in the town of Skradin, where the Krka River meets the Adriatic Sea.

## Primary Attractions Inside the Park

### Skradinski Buk

Skradinski Buk is the largest and most famous waterfall system in the park, consisting of 17 travertine steps spread over 800 meters. The elevation drops a total of 45.7 meters. This area is explored via a 1.9-kilometer circular wooden boardwalk that routes visitors over the rushing water, through dense forest, and past numerous smaller cascades before arriving at the large final plunge pool.

Walking the loop at a normal pace takes roughly an hour. Along the trail, restored 19th-century watermills function as small ethnographic museums demonstrating how locals historically ground grain and washed textiles. Near the main falls lie the remains of the Jaruga Hydroelectric Power Plant. Built in 1895, it was the second alternating current hydroelectric plant in the world, opening just two days after the one at Niagara Falls.

### Roški Slap

Located 22.5 kilometers upstream from Skradinski Buk, Roški Slap is the second most visited section of the park. This area features a massive 22.5-meter main waterfall and a series of smaller, parallel cascades known locally as the 'Necklaces.' The terrain here is wider and more open, with several hiking trails branching into the surrounding canyon.

Above the falls sits Oziđana Pećina, a prehistoric cave accessible via a steep climb of 517 wooden steps. Archaeological excavations here have uncovered ceramic fragments and stone tools indicating human presence dating back to 5000 BCE.

### Visovac Island and Monastery

Visovac Island sits in the middle of a lake-like expansion of the Krka River, positioned between Skradinski Buk and Roški Slap. The island is home to the Franciscan Monastery of Our Lady of Mercy and the Church of Our Lady of Visovac, established in 1445. The monastery houses an extensive library with rare books, historical manuscripts, and a collection of church linens.

Access to Visovac is strictly by authorized park boats. Visitors can book a two-hour excursion from Skradinski Buk, which includes a 30-minute guided tour of the island. Shorter boat rides are also available from the Stinice and Remetić boat docks on the mainland shores directly across from the island.

### Burnum and the Krka Eco Campus

In the remote northern section of the park, the remains of the Roman military camp Burnum overlook the river canyon. Originally established in the 1st century CE to control the river crossing, the site features the arches of a military command building and a recently excavated amphitheater capable of seating 8,000 spectators.

Nearby, the Krka Eco Campus in Puljane serves as the park's primary educational center. It features modern archaeological and natural history exhibits detailing the formation of the karst landscape and displaying artifacts recovered from the riverbed and Burnum.

## Navigating the Entrances

Krka National Park has five official entrances, but the vast majority of visitors use either Skradin or Lozovac.

### The Skradin Entrance

The town of Skradin sits 3.5 kilometers downriver from Skradinski Buk. Visitors arriving here purchase their tickets at the park office in the town center. From April through October, the entrance fee includes a 25-minute boat ride up the river to the base of the falls. The boats depart on a schedule, usually leaving Skradin on the hour and returning from the falls on the half-hour.

While official literature emphasizes the boat ride from Skradin, walking the 3.4-kilometer riverside trail is a far better option that bypasses the chaotic boarding queues entirely. The trail is flat, paved with fine gravel, and shaded by trees. Bicycles are also permitted on this path.

### The Lozovac Entrance

Lozovac is located on the plateau above Skradinski Buk. This entrance features a massive, free parking lot capable of accommodating hundreds of cars and tour buses. Because of the ample parking, Lozovac is the preferred entry point for independent drivers and large group tours.

From April to October, the park operates continuous shuttle buses to transport visitors down the steep access road to the ethno-village and the start of the boardwalk loop. During the winter months, visitors are permitted to drive their own vehicles down this road to park directly at the trailhead. Alternatively, a steep, rocky 875-meter pedestrian trail connects the Lozovac parking lot to the waterfalls.

### Minor Entrances

Visitors prioritizing the northern sights often bypass Skradin and Lozovac completely. Entrances at Roški Slap, Burnum, and Kistanje offer direct road access to these specific locations. Parking at these sites is generally free, and the entry gates rarely experience the long lines common at the southern access points.

## Comparing Krka to Plitvice Lakes

Travelers frequently weigh visiting Krka against Plitvice Lakes National Park, located 160 kilometers to the north. Both protect karst river systems and feature travertine waterfalls, but they offer distinct experiences.

Plitvice Lakes is significantly larger, requiring five to eight hours to walk its main routes. It strictly forbids swimming anywhere within its boundaries and features a higher concentration of connected lakes.

Krka is highly accessible for shorter visits. The main loop at Skradinski Buk can be completed in under two hours, making it an easy half-day excursion from coastal cities. Krka also incorporates cultural and historical elements—such as the Visovac monastery, watermills, and Roman ruins—that are absent from the purely natural landscape of Plitvice.

## Crowds, Weather, and Best Times to Visit

Krka National Park receives over one million visitors annually, with the vast majority arriving in July and August. During these months, the daily visitor count frequently reaches the park's absolute cap of 10,000 concurrent visitors at Skradinski Buk.

In peak summer, the narrow wooden boardwalks experience heavy pedestrian traffic, making it difficult to maintain a steady walking pace or take clear photographs. Temperatures frequently exceed 32°C (90°F), and the canyon traps humidity, making the hike uncomfortable during midday hours.

The optimal time to visit is during the shoulder seasons. In May, June, September, and October, the water levels are robust, the weather is mild, and the crowds are manageable. Furthermore, the €20 ticket price during these months represents a much better value for the experience provided.

Winter visits provide absolute solitude. The surrounding vegetation loses its leaves, offering unobstructed views of the waterfalls and the underlying rock formations. While the entry fee is only €7, the ferry from Skradin and the internal shuttle buses do not operate. Visitors must either drive directly to the trailheads or walk the access paths.

## Wildlife and Ecology of the River Basin

The Krka River basin is a highly protected ecosystem that supports significant biodiversity. The mixture of Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean climates creates favorable conditions for a wide variety of flora and fauna. Scientists have recorded over 1,000 species and subspecies of plants within the park boundaries. The limestone canyons are heavily vegetated with hornbeam, downy oak, and black ash trees, while the riverbanks feature dense reed beds and sedges.

Animal life is equally abundant. The river itself contains 20 species of fish, 10 of which are endemic to the Adriatic river systems. The brown trout and the Dalmatian barbelgudgeon are frequently spotted in the clear pools near the falls. The park is also recognized as an important ornithological area. Over 220 bird species either nest in the park or use it as a resting point during seasonal migrations. Golden eagles, short-toed snake eagles, and peregrine falcons hunt along the canyon walls. Amphibians and reptiles, including the European green toad and the Hermann's tortoise, inhabit the underbrush. Mammal populations include the European otter, wildcats, and 18 distinct species of bats that roost in the karst caves, such as the endangered long-fingered bat.

## Food and Dining Options Inside the Park

Visitors planning a full-day trip will find several food and beverage facilities operating within the park, primarily concentrated around the major entrances and attractions.

At the Skradinski Buk area, multiple concession stands and casual eateries operate during the peak and shoulder seasons. These establishments serve standard fast food, including sausages, burgers, sandwiches, and fries, alongside cold beverages and ice cream. Prices at these locations are notably marked up compared to restaurants outside the park. A standard lunch of a burger and a soda can cost upwards of €15 to €20.

At Roški Slap, the dining options are slightly more traditional. Local vendors sell domestic products, and there is a well-known rustic restaurant that serves platters of air-dried Dalmatian prosciutto, local sheep cheese, and homemade bread.

Despite the available options, many visitors choose to pack their own food. Picnic tables are available in designated rest areas near Skradinski Buk and the Lozovac ethno-village. Bringing a refillable water bottle is highly recommended. The summer heat in the canyon is intense, and purchasing multiple bottles of water at the concession stands quickly becomes expensive. Free drinking water fountains are located near the restrooms at the main access points.

## Packing and Preparation

Proper preparation heavily influences the quality of a visit to Krka National Park. Given the uneven terrain and the extensive walking involved, sturdy, comfortable footwear is essential. While the main boardwalks at Skradinski Buk are relatively flat, the connecting paths, the steep trails at Lozovac, and the hundreds of stairs at Oziđana Pećina require shoes with solid grip. Flip-flops are highly impractical and increase the risk of injury on the slippery wooden planks.

During the summer months, sun protection is critical. Much of the Skradin walking trail and the boat decks offer no shade. Visitors should pack high-SPF sunscreen, wide-brimmed hats, and sunglasses. Because swimming is banned at the main falls, swimwear is only necessary if visitors plan to swim at the designated beach in Skradin or the specific zones near Roški Slap.

Travelers arriving independently should carry a mix of cash and credit cards. While the main ticket offices accept digital payments, small vendors selling ice cream, souvenirs, and independent bus operators frequently operate on a cash-only basis.

## How to Get to Krka National Park

The park is highly connected to the Dalmatian coast, making it a standard stop for tourists stationed in Split, Zadar, and Šibenik.

**From Šibenik:** Krka is exceptionally close to Šibenik, located just 17 kilometers inland. The drive takes less than 20 minutes via local roads to either the Lozovac or Skradin entrance. Public buses run regularly from the Šibenik main bus station to Skradin, costing approximately €3 to €5 per direction.

**From Split:** The drive from Split covers 90 kilometers and takes roughly 1 hour and 15 minutes via the E65 toll motorway. The toll costs approximately €4. Dozens of tour operators in Split offer half-day excursions to Krka, providing round-trip bus transport and an English-speaking guide for roughly €30 to €40, though the park entrance fee is almost always collected separately in cash.

**From Zadar:** Krka is situated 80 kilometers southeast of Zadar. The drive takes about one hour on the E65 motorway. Public buses from Zadar to Skradin operate several times daily, with a travel time of one hour.

## The Final Verdict: Is It Worth It?

Determining if Krka National Park is worth the trip depends heavily on timing. For travelers visiting in the shoulder season, the €20 admission fee provides excellent access to a major European natural site, well-maintained infrastructure, and unique cultural history.

In peak summer, the value equation shifts. A family of four will pay nearly €110 for admission alone, not factoring in transportation, food, or optional boat excursions. The dense crowds on the primary boardwalks can turn a nature walk into a slow-moving shuffle.

Those deciding to visit during July and August should arrive at the entry gates exactly when they open at 8:00 AM. Completing the Skradinski Buk loop before 10:00 AM ensures a much calmer experience before the massive tour buses arrive from Split and Zadar. Alternatively, arriving after 3:00 PM provides softer lighting for photography and slightly thinner crowds as early visitors depart.

Krka National Park remains a spectacular display of hydrogeology and history. As long as visitors calibrate their expectations regarding the swimming regulations and the summer pricing, it stands as a top destination on the Adriatic coast.

faq.question: Can you swim in Krka National Park in 2027?
faq.answer: Swimming at the famous Skradinski Buk waterfall has been strictly prohibited since January 2021 to protect the ecosystem. However, visitors can still swim in designated areas at Roški Slap between June and September, or at the public beach in the nearby town of Skradin.

faq.question: How much is the entrance fee to Krka National Park?
faq.answer: During the peak summer months from June through September, adult admission is €40. The price drops to €20 in the shoulder season months of April, May, and October, and costs just €7 during the winter months from November to March.

faq.question: How long does it take to visit Krka National Park?
faq.answer: Most visitors spend between three to four hours in the park to complete the 1.9-kilometer Skradinski Buk boardwalk loop and take the boat ride from Skradin. Exploring the northern sections like Roški Slap or taking a boat to Visovac Island will extend the visit to a full day.

faq.question: Which entrance is better: Skradin or Lozovac?
faq.answer: Lozovac is the best entrance for those driving, as it features a massive free parking lot and a quick shuttle bus down to the falls. The Skradin entrance is ideal for visitors who want to arrive at the waterfalls via the park's official ferry boat or the 3.4-kilometer riverside walking trail.

faq.question: Do you need hiking boots for Krka National Park?
faq.answer: Heavy hiking boots are not necessary for the main Skradinski Buk loop, as the path consists of flat wooden boardwalks and packed gravel. However, comfortable walking shoes with good grip are essential, as the wooden planks can become slippery near the waterfalls.

faq.question: How do you get from Split to Krka National Park?
faq.answer: The drive from Split to Krka takes about 1 hour and 15 minutes via the E65 toll motorway, covering roughly 90 kilometers. Dozens of bus companies and tour operators in Split also run daily half-day trips that cost between €30 and €40 for round-trip transport.

quickAnswer: Krka National Park is worth visiting for its extensive waterfalls and historic boat trips, but the €40 summer entrance fee and permanent swimming ban at the main falls disappoint some visitors. To avoid massive crowds and justify the cost, visit during shoulder season when tickets cost €20.
